title: Review: Electric and magnetic fields
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: D.2#c22 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2#c16 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2#c12 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: D.2#q33, D.2#q06, D.2#q08, D.2#q12, D.2#q14, D.2#q16, D.2#q18, D.2#q05, D.2#q10, D.2#q11, D.2#q34, D.2#q15, D.2#q35, D.2#q36, D.2#q38, D.2#q27, D.2#q28, D.2#q30. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Right-hand grip rule
items.clue: Thumb along the current; curled fingers give the direction of the field.

items.label: Electric field line
items.clue: Its direction at each point is that of the force on a positive test charge.

items.label: Electric charge
items.clue: A property of matter of two types, positive and negative; like repel, unlike attract.

items.label: Electrostatic induction
items.clue: A nearby charged object rearranges the free charge in a conductor without touching it.

questions.stem: In an experiment of Millikan's type, an oil drop of weight 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N is held stationary between two horizontal parallel plates 5.0 mm apart, with a potential difference of 500 V across them. The field between the plates is uniform. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the charge on the drop?
questions.explanation: E = V/d = 500/0.0050 = 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. For the drop to be stationary, qE = W, so q = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.0 × 10⁵ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This is exactly 3 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: a whole-number multiple of e, as quantization of charge requires.

questions.stem: A polythene rod becomes negatively charged when it is rubbed with a woollen cloth. Which statement explains how the rod becomes charged?

options.text: Rubbing creates new negative charge in the surface layer of the rod.
Protons move from the rod to the cloth, leaving the rod with a negative charge.
Electrons move from the cloth to the rod, so the rod gains extra electrons.
Electrons move from the rod to the cloth, as negative means a lack of electrons.

questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons between the surfaces. The rod gains electrons (an excess makes it negative) and the cloth loses the same number, becoming equally positive: charge is conserved.

questions.stem: Which statement defines the electric field strength at a point?

options.text: The force on any charged object that is placed at that point, measured in newtons.
The force per unit charge on any small charge, in the direction of the force on it.
The energy per unit charge transferred to a small charge placed at that point.
The force per unit charge exerted on a small positive test charge placed at that point.

questions.explanation: E = F/q, defined using a small positive test charge, so that the test charge does not disturb the source charges and the direction of E is the direction of the force on a positive charge. Unit: N C⁻¹.

questions.stem: A hollow metal sphere on an insulating stand is given a positive charge. Which description of the electric field lines is correct?

options.text: Lines inside as well as outside, since the charge is spread through the whole sphere.
None inside; outside, radial lines pointing away, as if from a point charge at the centre.
Lines leave the surface both ways, pointing inwards and outwards from the charge.
None inside; outside, parallel and equally spaced lines, as the charge is spread evenly.

questions.stem: The field lines of an isolated negative point charge spread out in three dimensions, and the same number of lines passes through every sphere centred on the charge. Point P is 2.0 cm from the charge and point Q is 6.0 cm from it. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 3 times E at Q, as P is 3 times closer, so the lines are 3 times as close.
E is the same at P and Q, as each line that passes P's sphere also passes Q's sphere.
E at P is 9 times E at Q, as there are 9 times as many lines per unit area at P.
E cannot be compared, as the number of field lines drawn is merely an arbitrary choice.

questions.stem: Two parallel plates remain connected to the same supply while their separation is doubled. A small charged dust particle is held between the plates, well away from their edges. How does the electric force on the particle change?

options.text: It is unchanged, since E depends only on V, which the supply fixes.
It halves, since E = V/d and d has doubled while V is unchanged.
It falls to a quarter, since E ∝ 1/d², like the field of a point charge.
It doubles, since E = Vd and d has doubled at constant V.

questions.explanation: The supply keeps V fixed. Between the plates E = V/d, so doubling d halves E, and F = qE halves.

questions.stem: A flat horizontal circular coil carries a steady current that flows anticlockwise when viewed from above. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the coil?

options.text: There is no field: the fields of opposite sides cancel out.
Vertically upwards, along the central axis of the coil.
Horizontal, in the plane of the coil, circling like the current.
Vertically downwards, along the central axis of the coil.

questions.explanation: Apply the right-hand grip rule to any part of the coil: with the thumb along the anticlockwise current, the curled fingers pass upwards through the inside of the loop. Every part gives an upward field at the centre, so the field there is vertically upwards, along the axis.

questions.stem: In an experiment of Millikan's type, the charges on four oil drops were measured in arbitrary units as 7.50, 12.5, 17.5 and 22.5 units. Assuming that electric charge is quantized, what is the largest value of the basic unit of charge that is consistent with all four results?

options.text: 7.50 units
2.50 units
15.0 units
5.00 units

questions.explanation: The basic unit must divide every charge a whole number of times. 7.50, 12.5, 17.5 and 22.5 are 3, 5, 7 and 9 times 2.50, and no larger value divides all four: 5.00 fails for 7.50 (1.5 units) and 7.50 fails for 12.5.

questions.stem: Two point charges of +4.0 nC and +1.0 nC are fixed 0.30 m apart. At one point on the line between them the resultant electric field strength is zero. How far is this point from the +4.0 nC charge?
questions.explanation: At the neutral point the two fields are equal and opposite: k(4.0 nC)/x² = k(1.0 nC)/(0.30 − x)². Taking square roots, x/(0.30 − x) = 2, so x = 0.20 m from the +4.0 nC charge (0.10 m from the +1.0 nC charge).

questions.stem: A student sketches the electric field lines around two equal positive point charges a short distance apart. Which description of a correct sketch is right?

options.text: Lines leave each charge and curve away from the other, with a neutral point at the midpoint.
Lines leave each charge, and some of them cross one another in the region midway between them.
Lines run from one charge to the other, joining the two charges across the gap.
Straight radial lines leave each charge, exactly as if the other charge were absent.

questions.stem: A sketch shows the electric field lines near a charged object. A small positive test charge is placed at a point P that lies midway between two neighbouring field lines, in a region where the lines are closely spaced. Which statement is correct?

options.text: No force acts on it at P, since the electric field exists only along the lines that are drawn.
A force acts on it at P, but its size cannot be judged, as the number of lines drawn is a matter of choice.
A force acts on it at P, of the same size as anywhere between those two lines, as the field is constant along a line.
A force acts on it at P, and the close spacing of the lines shows that the field there is relatively strong.

questions.stem: Two parallel metal plates 5.0 mm apart in a vacuum are connected to a 1500 V supply. An electron is between the plates, well away from their edges. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the magnitude of the electric force on the electron?

Three point charges, each of +2.0 nC, are brought from infinite separation and fixed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.10 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the total work done by the external forces to assemble the system?
questions.explanation: Bringing in the first charge needs no work. The second needs kq²/a = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J against the first. The third needs kq²/a against each of the two already there, 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ J. Total: 3 pairs × 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ J = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ J.

questions.stem: Two point charges, +q and −q, are held a distance r apart, with electric potential energy zero at infinite separation. The separation is then increased to 2r. Which statement about the electric potential energy E_p of the system is correct?

options.text: E_p rises from −kq²/r to −kq²/2r, so an external force does positive work on it.
E_p falls from −kq²/r to −kq²/2r, because its size has been halved.
E_p changes from −kq²/r to −kq²/4r, because it obeys an inverse-square law.
E_p falls from +kq²/r to +kq²/2r, because potential energy is a positive quantity.

questions.explanation: E_p = kq₁q₂/r = −kq²/r at separation r and −kq²/2r at 2r. Since −kq²/2r is greater (less negative) than −kq²/r, E_p increases; the increase is supplied by positive work from the external force pulling the unlike charges apart.

questions.stem: A metal sphere of diameter 0.20 m carries a charge of +6.0 nC, spread uniformly over its surface. Electric potential is zero at infinity. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at a point 0.20 m from the surface of the sphere?
questions.explanation: The distance in V_e = kQ/r is measured from the centre of the sphere: r = radius + 0.20 m = 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30 m. V_e = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30 = 1.8 × 10² V.

questions.stem: A point charge of +5.0 nC is fixed in place. A second charge of +2.0 nC is moved slowly from a point 0.30 m from the fixed charge to a point 0.10 m from it. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the work done on the +2.0 nC charge by the external force?
Equipotential surfaces are drawn at equal steps of potential. Which description is correct for the arrangement named?

options.text: Between oppositely charged parallel plates: evenly spaced planes parallel to the plates.
Around an isolated point charge: concentric spheres, evenly spaced from the charge outwards.
Inside a charged hollow metal sphere: the potential is zero everywhere, as the field is zero.
Near two equal positive point charges: curves that follow the field lines out from the charges.

questions.explanation: Between the plates (away from the edges) E is uniform, so V changes by equal amounts in equal distances: the equipotentials are equally spaced planes parallel to the plates, perpendicular to the field lines.

questions.stem: A small positive charge is moved along an equipotential surface in the electric field of a fixed point charge. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The field is perpendicular to its path, so the field does no work on the charge.
There is no electric field on the surface, so no force acts on the charge at all.
The field does work on the charge, as the electric force acts on it throughout.
The field acts along the surface, in the same direction as the charge moves.

questions.explanation: Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, so the electric force is perpendicular to the displacement: W = Fs cos 90° = 0. Equivalently, W = qΔV_e = 0 because ΔV_e = 0 along the surface.
